Headlines: Unfair to Christians if concert put off Live public access to 40pc revenue appeal Oct 29 Sabah’s 40pc grant never linked to political support City Hall eyes carbon revenue Sungai Bunus undergoing a makeover Published on: Tuesday, March 24, 2015 Published on: Tue, Mar 24, 2015 Text Size: Dark Mode: Off Text: Dark Mode: Off Kuala Lumpur: Though Kuala Lumpur has yet to experience another massive floods since the last one in 1971, flash floods have been recurring over the years. The worst flash floods occurred in 2007, during which several locations in the city were submerged under a metre of water. Areas such as Jalan Masjid India, Jalan Ipoh, Kampung Baru, Kampung Chubadak and Sentul were badly affected at the time. The following major flash flood of a similar proportion was on Dec 13, 2011, which affected major roads surrounding Jalan Tun Razak due to spillover from Sungai Bunus. Advertisement The Sungai Bunus catchment is located within the city and is a reason why the river contributes to floods in Kuala Lumpur. The Wisma Bernama building in Jalan Tun Razak is one of the areas often affected by floods. Read more For Bernama employees, they have become used to the rising water levels at Sungai Bunus that is just roughly 50 metres away. An it was almost like a routine for the staff to rush out and remove their cars from the parking lot when the water in Sg Bunus reaches a critical level after a heavy rain. In the 2007 floods, many vehicles were damaged as the water rose rapidly leaving no time for the staff to remove their cars. Advertisement Sungai Bunus is one of Sungai Klang's 11 major tributaries and measures about nine kilometres long. It runs from Setapak, Wangsa Maju and Setiawangsa, through Kampung Baru and the heart of Kuala Lumpur near the Jamek Mosque before it enters Sungai Klang. The river also flows within landmarks including Kampung Baru, National Library, National Heart Institute, National Art Gallery, Istana Budaya, Taman Titiwangsa, Chow Kit Market and Kolej Universiti Tuanku Abdul Rahman, Setapak. Advertisement However, only about 5.5 kilometres of Sungai Bunus is visible while the remaining, starting from the TH Selborn building until the city centre, is concealed and flows underground. Many are not aware that they are crossing over Sungai Bunus as some parts of the town, such as in Kampung Periuk near the Sultan Sulaiman Hall in Kampung Baru as it has been tarred over above. According to a Kg Baru resident who only wants to be known as Hj Din, there was a narrow crossing dubbed 'jambatan gesel' over the river and the passing damsels grazed the youths waiting on the bridge as it was so narrow. Over the years the river had experienced hydrological changes and became smaller and narrower. When there is no rain, the river is only a place where sewage flows. When it rains, water does not seep into the soil or flow into the river which causes runoff and lead to floods. This is the situation faced by Sungai Bunus and Sungai Klang's other tributaries. The floods in 2011 expedited the Sungai Bunus Flood Mitigation Project carried out by the Department of Irrigation and Drainage in early 2013. The project is an integrated effort under the River Of Life (ROL) project and Kuala Lumpur City Hall's Local Agenda 21. The flood mitigation project will reduce the volume of water in Sungai Bunus, especially during heavy downpours, to prevent spillover into Sungai Klang and contribute to floods in Kuala Lumpur, said project consultant Azman Abu Bakar. For example, Sungai Bunus received 220 cubic metres of water per second during the floods in 2011, compared to its capacity of 70 cubic metres per second. "In 2011, water from Sungai Bunus overflowed while water in Sungai Klang reached its maximum, preventing water from Sungai Bunus from entering Sungai Klang. This project will help to reduce water flow by 70 to 80 per cent," he said. The RM160 million project is 30 percent complete covering the Sungai Bunus diversion, Kg Boyan catchment, Kuala Lumpur Police Training Centre (Pulapol) catchment, Air Leleh catchment, Setapak Jaya catchment, Sri Rampai catchment and Air Panas catchment. Turning rivers into a tourist attraction will benefit Kuala Lumpur and its residents. Imagine giving each catchment a new look and a recreational centre that offers the public a variety of facilities. Constructing gates at the catchment is among the methods that will be used to control the water level at Sungai Bunus to a specific level when there is no rain. According to Azman this would revive the river as well as restore its ecosystem. "A walkway will be built along Sungai Bunus to allow recreational activities while enjoying the beauty of the landscape. "We hope this teaches the public to appreciate rivers and not to treat it as a dump," he said, adding that they faced challenges in efforts to sustain Sungai Bunus. The lack of reserve land in several areas along Sungai Bunus has prevented efforts for total beautification of the river. "There should be some reserve land. However, due to lack of planning in river preservation, land by the river have been used up for commercial purposes," he said. Besides beautifying the river, an underground museum is planned next to the Sungai Bunus diversion in Jalan Tun Razak. The museum will be of interest to people who want to know more about the river. The entrance to the museum will be located behind the TH Selborn building and visitors will exit in front of the Petronas station in Kampung Baru. "We will work with the Historical Society to gather material on Sungai Bunus for us to display and enliven the river," he said. The museum is expected to be ready by the year-end. – Bernama Stay up-to-date by following Daily Express's Telegram channel.
